question: Bohr's semiclassical model of the hydrogen atom assumed that the ground state angular momentum of the electron is $\hbar=h /(2 \pi)$. While this model is incorrect, the Bohr radius does give the correct lengthscale of the hydrogen atom. By analogy to the Bohr model, consider a bound system consisting of a neutron and an electron interacting purely gravitationally. If the orbital angular momentum is $\hbar$, what would be the radius of this "atom"?
answer: This question was inspired by a comment in Professor Ethan Neil's quantum mechanics class. The electron mass is sufficiently small compared to that of the neutron that we can neglect the fact that both particles orbit about their combined center of mass and treat the neutron as stationary, although it is not difficult to take that into account using the reduced mass. Setting the gravitational force equal to centripetal acceleration with $L=m_{e} v r=\hbar$ (2 points), $$ \frac{G m_{n} m_{e}}{r^{2}}=\frac{m_{e} v^{2}}{r}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m_{e} r^{3}} $$ (2 points) so $$ \begin{aligned} r & =\frac{\hbar^{2}}{G m_{n} m_{e}^{2}}=\frac{\left(6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}\right)^{2}}{4 \pi^{2}\left(6.674 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}^{3} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)\left(1.675 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}\right)\left(9.110 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}\right)^{2}} & =1.2 \times 10^{29} \mathrm{~m} \cdot \frac{1 \text { light year }}{9.461 \times 10^{15} \mathrm{~m}}=1.3 \times 10^{13} \text { light years } \end{aligned} $$ which is significantly larger than the observable universe! This illustrates the relative weakness of the gravitational force compared to electromagnetism. (3 points for final expression for $r, \mathbf{3}$ points for final calculation - meters is fine)

question: An observer is located at latitude $\phi=+42.0^{\circ}$ (Northern Hemisphere). Assume the Earth is a perfect sphere and ignore atmospheric refraction. Star $A$ has equatorial coordinates $$ \alpha=6^{\mathrm{h}} 40^{\mathrm{m}}, \quad \delta=+62.0^{\circ} $$ On a particular night, the local sidereal time (LST) is $$ \mathrm{LST}=5^{\mathrm{h}} 10^{\mathrm{m}} $$ at 10:00 PM local clock time. You may assume that one sidereal day equals $23^{\mathrm{h}} 56^{\mathrm{m}}$ of clock time. Compute the hour angle $H$ of star $A$ at 10:00 PM. State whether the star is east or west of the meridian at that moment.
answer: Hour angle and sky side. (2 points) Convert to hours: $$ \alpha=6^{\mathrm{h}} 40^{\mathrm{m}}=6.666 \overline{6} \mathrm{~h}, \quad \mathrm{LST}=5^{\mathrm{h}} 10^{\mathrm{m}}=5.166 \overline{6} \mathrm{~h} . $$ Thus $$ H=5^{\mathrm{h}} 10^{\mathrm{m}}-6^{\mathrm{h}} 40^{\mathrm{m}}=-1^{\mathrm{h}} 30^{\mathrm{m}} . $$ Since $H<0$, the star is east of the meridian. Equivalently, in degrees ( $15^{\circ}$ per hour): $$ H=-1.5 \mathrm{~h} \times 15^{\circ} / \mathrm{h}=-22.5^{\circ} $$ Accept answers in range: $-22.5^{\circ} \pm 0.3^{\circ}$.

question: An observer is located at latitude $\phi=+42.0^{\circ}$ (Northern Hemisphere). Assume the Earth is a perfect sphere and ignore atmospheric refraction. Star $A$ has equatorial coordinates $$ \alpha=6^{\mathrm{h}} 40^{\mathrm{m}}, \quad \delta=+62.0^{\circ} $$ On a particular night, the local sidereal time (LST) is $$ \mathrm{LST}=5^{\mathrm{h}} 10^{\mathrm{m}} $$ at 10:00 PM local clock time. You may assume that one sidereal day equals $23^{\mathrm{h}} 56^{\mathrm{m}}$ of clock time. ( $\mathbf{5}$ points) Compute the altitude $h$ of star $A$ at 10:00 PM. Give your answer in degrees.
answer: Altitude at 10:00 PM. (5 points) Using spherical law of cosines, $$ \sin h=\sin \phi \sin \delta+\cos \phi \cos \delta \cos H $$ Substitute $\phi=42^{\circ}, \delta=62^{\circ}, H=-22.5^{\circ}$ : $$ \sin h=\sin 42^{\circ} \sin 62^{\circ}+\cos 42^{\circ} \cos 62^{\circ} \cos \left(22.5^{\circ}\right) $$ Numerically, $$ \sin h \approx 0.9131 $$ Therefore, $$ h \approx \arcsin (0.9131) \approx 65.9^{\circ} . $$ Accept answers between $65^{\circ}$ and $67^{\circ}$. Grading: 5 pts: Correct substitution, trig evaluation, and final altitude. 4 pts: Correct setup with minor arithmetic error. 3 pts: Correct formula but computational errors. 2 pts: Some progress towards Eq. 3 but incorrect substitution and arithmetic errors. 1 pt: Partial substitution or wrong angle sign. 0 pts: No correct use of relation. Note: If a student forgets $\cos (-H)=\cos H$, do not deduct heavily unless the conceptual reasoning is affected.

question: An observer is located at latitude $\phi=+42.0^{\circ}$ (Northern Hemisphere). Assume the Earth is a perfect sphere and ignore atmospheric refraction. Star $A$ has equatorial coordinates $$ \alpha=6^{\mathrm{h}} 40^{\mathrm{m}}, \quad \delta=+62.0^{\circ} $$ On a particular night, the local sidereal time (LST) is $$ \mathrm{LST}=5^{\mathrm{h}} 10^{\mathrm{m}} $$ at 10:00 PM local clock time. You may assume that one sidereal day equals $23^{\mathrm{h}} 56^{\mathrm{m}}$ of clock time. ( $\mathbf{5}$ points) For star $B$, compute the total clock-time duration during which the star is above the horizon during one sidereal day. Express your final answer in hours and minutes of clock time.
answer: Time above the horizon. (5 points) Use the horizon condition $$ \cos H_{0}=-\tan \phi \tan \delta, $$ which comes from Eq. 3 with altitude $h=0$. Substitute $\phi=42^{\circ}, \delta=30^{\circ}$ : $$ \cos H_{0}=-\tan 42^{\circ} \tan 30^{\circ} $$ Using $$ \begin{gathered} \tan 42^{\circ} \approx 0.900, \quad \tan 30^{\circ} \approx 0.577, \cos H_{0} \approx-0.519 . \end{gathered} $$ Thus $$ H_{0} \approx \cos ^{-1}(-0.519) \approx 121.3^{\circ} . $$ Convert to hours: $$ H_{0}=\frac{121.3^{\circ}}{15^{\circ} / \text { hour }} \approx 8.09 \text { hours. } $$ The star is above the horizon for $$ 2 H_{0} \approx 16.18 \text { sidereal hours. } $$ Convert to clock time using $$ \begin{gathered} \text { 1 sidereal hour } \approx 59^{\mathrm{m}} 50^{\mathrm{s}} . 16.18 \times 59^{\mathrm{m}} 50^{\mathrm{s}} \approx 16^{\mathrm{h}} 08^{\mathrm{m}} . \text { Star is above the horizon for about } 16^{\mathrm{h}} 08^{\mathrm{m}} . \end{gathered} $$

question: An astronomer who enjoys solar observations has the habit of recording the Sun's right ascension and declination every day. These coordinates are always recorded at the same civil time (the time on the clock). Between two consecutive observations, which happened when the Sun was in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere, the declination of the Sun increased by $0.3650^{\circ}$. Estimate the days in which these two observations occurred. Neglect the eccentricity of Earth's orbit.
answer: \subsection*{First Approach} In order to estimate the days of the observations, the first step is to determine the declination of the Sun at the point in which its rate of variation in declination is $0.3650^{\circ} /$ day. Note that there are two such points in the celestial sphere, but since the problem statement specifies that the Sun was in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere, it is possible to obtain an unique solution. Using the figure below, it is possible to obtain an expression for angle $x$, which can be used to break down the angular velocity of the Sun into a right ascension component and a declination component. Using the spherical law of sines: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\sin x}{\sin \left(90^{\circ}-\varepsilon\right)} & =\frac{\sin 90^{\circ}}{\sin \left(90^{\circ}-\delta\right)} \sin x & =\frac{\cos \varepsilon}{\cos \delta} \end{aligned} $$ Using the Pythagorean trigonometric identity: $$ \cos x=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\cos \varepsilon}{\cos \delta}\right)^{2}} $$ Neglecting the eccentricity of the Earth's orbit, the angular velocity of the Sun on the Ecliptic corresponds to $\omega=\frac{360^{\circ}}{365.2564 \text { days }}=0.98561^{\circ} /$ day . The declination component of the angular velocity ( $\omega_{\delta}$ ) can be obtained through the following expression: $$ \begin{aligned} \omega_{\delta} & =\omega \cos x \frac{\omega_{\delta}}{\omega} & =\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\cos \varepsilon}{\cos \delta}\right)^{2}} \frac{\cos \varepsilon}{\cos \delta} & = \pm \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega_{\delta}}{\omega}\right)^{2}} \cos \delta & = \pm \frac{\cos \varepsilon}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{\omega_{\delta}}{\omega}\right)^{2}}} \cos \delta & = \pm \frac{\cos 23.44^{\circ}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{0.365}{0.98561}\right)^{2}}} \cos \delta & = \pm 0.9877 \end{aligned} $$ Since the Sun is in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere and the change in declination is positive, the Sun must be in the first quadrant of the Ecliptic. Therefore: $$ \begin{aligned} \cos \delta & =0.9877 \delta & =8.995^{\circ} \end{aligned} $$ The next step is to find the ecliptic longitude of the Sun. Using the spherical law of sines: $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\sin \lambda}{\sin 90^{\circ}} & =\frac{\sin \delta}{\sin \varepsilon} \sin \lambda & =\frac{\sin 8.995^{\circ}}{\sin 23.44^{\circ}} \sin \lambda & =0.3930 \lambda & =23.14^{\circ} \end{aligned} $$ Since the angular velocity of the Sun throughout the ecliptic is constant if Earth's orbital eccentricity is constant, it is possible to obtain the number of days since the vernal equinox: $$ \begin{aligned} \lambda & =\omega d d & =\frac{\lambda}{\omega} d & =\frac{23.14^{\circ}}{0.98561^{\circ} / \text { day }} d & =23.48 \text { days } \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the observation corresponds to days 23 and 24 after the vernal equinox. Since the vernal equinox occurs around March $20^{\text {th }}$, the observations correspond to April $12^{\text {th }}$ and April $13{ }^{\text {th }}$. Since the equinox does not necessarily happen on March $20^{\text {th }}$, pairs of days between April $10^{\text {th }}$ and April $15^{\text {th }}$ are acceptable without any point deductions. It is also possible to solve this problem in an alternative way. Consider the following expression, which can be obtained through the law of sines for spherical triangles: $$ \sin \delta=\sin \varepsilon \sin \lambda $$ Deriving this expression with respect to time: $$ \begin{aligned} \cos \delta \frac{\mathrm{d} \delta}{\mathrm{~d} t} & =\sin \varepsilon \cos \lambda \frac{\mathrm{d} \lambda}{\mathrm{~d} t} \sqrt{1-\sin ^{2} \delta} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \delta}{\mathrm{~d} t} & =\sin \varepsilon \cos \lambda \frac{\mathrm{d} \lambda}{\mathrm{~d} t} \sqrt{1-(\sin \varepsilon \sin \lambda)^{2}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \delta}{\mathrm{~d} t} & =\sin \varepsilon \cos \lambda \frac{\mathrm{d} \lambda}{\mathrm{~d} t} {\left[1-(\sin \varepsilon \sin \lambda)^{2}\right]\left(\frac{\mathrm{d} \delta}{\mathrm{~d} t}\right)^{2} } & =\sin ^{2} \varepsilon \cos ^{2} \lambda\left(\frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{~d} t}\right)^{2} \end{aligned} $$ The rate $\frac{\mathrm{d} \lambda}{\mathrm{d} t}$ is constant and corresponds to $\frac{360^{\circ}}{365.2564 \text { days }}=0.98561^{\circ} /$ day. Based on the problem statement, $\frac{\mathrm{d} \delta}{\mathrm{d} t}=0.3650^{\circ} /$ day. In order to simplify the expression, it is convenient to define a variable $k=\left(\frac{\mathrm{d} \lambda}{\mathrm{d} t}\right)^{2} /\left(\frac{\mathrm{d} \delta}{\mathrm{d} t}\right)^{2} \approx 7.29$. Therefore: $$ \begin{aligned} 1-\sin ^{2} \varepsilon \sin ^{2} \lambda & =k \sin ^{2} \varepsilon \cos ^{2} \lambda 1 & =\sin ^{2} \varepsilon\left(\sin ^{2} \lambda+k \cos ^{2} \lambda\right) \frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \varepsilon} & =\sin ^{2} \lambda+k\left(1-\sin ^{2} \lambda\right) \frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \varepsilon} & =\sin ^{2} \lambda+k-k \sin ^{2} \lambda \frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \varepsilon} & =(1-k) \sin ^{2} \lambda+k \sin ^{2} \lambda & =\frac{1}{1-k}\left(\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \varepsilon}-k\right) \end{aligned} $$ Since the declination increased between the two observations and the Sun was in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere, $\lambda$ must be in the first quadrant. Therefore: $$ \begin{aligned} \sin ^{2} \lambda & =0.1545 \sin \lambda & =0.3930 \lambda & =23.14^{\circ} \end{aligned} $$ From this point onward, the solution follows the same steps as the first approach.

question: Enceladus is a moon of Saturn which has an outer crust of ice and is believed to have a subsurface liquid water ocean. Here are some useful physical properties: Figure 1: Cassini image of geysers from Enceladus. From NASA. The relevant physical properties are: Radius of Enceladus (including the ice shell): $R=250\ \mathrm{km}$. Ice shell thickness: $H=25\ \mathrm{km}$. Density of ice: $\rho_i=920\ \mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$. Surface gravity: $g=0.11\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, which may be treated as constant throughout the icy shell to the top of the subsurface ocean. Semi-major axis of Enceladus' orbit around Saturn: $a=2.4\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$. Mass of Saturn: $M=5.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The Cassini spacecraft observed that geysers of water erupt from the surface at a speed of $v=400\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ relative to Enceladus. Calculate whether this water has sufficient speed to escape the gravitational field of Enceladus. If so, will it remain gravitationally bound to Saturn or escape into solar orbit?
answer: We are not given the mass of Enceladus, but we know that $g=G m / R^{2}$. The escape velocity of Enceladus is (1 point for escape velocity formula, $\mathbf{2}$ points for rewriting in terms of known quantities, 2 points for calculation) $$ v_{e s c, E}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G m}{R}}=\sqrt{2 g R}=\sqrt{2\left(0.11 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\right)\left(250 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~m}\right)}=230 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}<v, $$ so the geyser can escape Enceladus ( $\mathbf{1}$ point). The escape velocity of Saturn from Enceladus is (1 point for formula, 1 point for calculation) $$ v_{e s c, S}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\left(6.674 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}^{3} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}\right)\left(5.7 \times 10^{26} \mathrm{~kg}\right)}{2.4 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m}}}=18,000 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}, $$ so even when added to the orbital speed of Enceladus (which is $v_{e s c, S} / \sqrt{2}$ ) ( $\mathbf{1}$ point for some mention that you need to change reference frames), $v$ is much too small. The material enters into orbit around Saturn. (1 point) This is the source of Saturn's E ring!

question: Enceladus is a moon of Saturn which has an outer crust of ice and is believed to have a subsurface liquid water ocean. Here are some useful physical properties: Figure 1: Cassini image of geysers from Enceladus. From NASA. The relevant physical properties are: Radius of Enceladus (including the ice shell): $R=250\ \mathrm{km}$. Ice shell thickness: $H=25\ \mathrm{km}$. Density of ice: $\rho_i=920\ \mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$. Surface gravity: $g=0.11\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, which may be treated as constant throughout the icy shell to the top of the subsurface ocean. Semi-major axis of Enceladus' orbit around Saturn: $a=2.4\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$. Mass of Saturn: $M=5.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Assuming that the water in the geysers starts from rest at the top of the subsurface ocean, calculate the pressure necessary to accelerate the water to $v=400\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$ at the surface of Enceladus, where there is no ambient pressure. Assume that viscous losses are negligible and the geyser material has a constant density of $1000\ \mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$, ignoring any phase changes.
answer: According to Bernoulli's principle, (2 points) $$ \frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2}+\rho g h+P $$ is a constant. Equating its value for the geyser at the top of the subsurface ocean and the surface of Enceladus, (1 point) $$ \frac{1}{2} \rho(0)^{2}-\rho g H+P=\frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2}+\rho g \cdot 0+0 $$ so ( $\mathbf{2}$ points for equation for pressure, $\mathbf{1}$ point for calculation) $P=\frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2}+\rho g H=\left(1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}(400 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})^{2}+\left(0.11 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\right)\left(25 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~m}\right)\right)=8.3 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{~Pa}$.

question: Enceladus is a moon of Saturn which has an outer crust of ice and is believed to have a subsurface liquid water ocean. The relevant physical properties are: Radius of Enceladus (including the ice shell): $R=250\ \mathrm{km}$. Ice shell thickness: $H=25\ \mathrm{km}$. Density of ice: $\rho_i=920\ \mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{m}^{3}$. Surface gravity: $g=0.11\ \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, which may be treated as constant throughout the icy shell to the top of the subsurface ocean. Semi-major axis of Enceladus' orbit around Saturn: $a=2.4\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$. Mass of Saturn: $M=5.7\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Estimate the hydrostatic pressure due to the weight of the icy shell at the top of the subsurface ocean. Is that pressure sufficient to explain the speed of the geysers?
answer: The pressure from the icy shell is ( $\mathbf{2}$ points for equation for pressure, $\mathbf{1}$ point for calculation) $$ \rho_{i} g H=\left(920 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}\right)\left(0.11 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\right)\left(25 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~m}\right)=2.5 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~Pa} $$ which is more than an order of magnitude too small. An alternative calculation of the pressure (either way receives full points) is $$ \frac{4}{3} \pi\left(R^{3}-(R-H)^{3}\right) \rho_{i} g /\left(4 \pi(R-H)^{2}\right)=2.8 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~Pa} $$ No, there must be some other source of pressure to accelerate the geysers. \paragraph{(1 point)} One possibility is that tidal forces from Saturn can lead to cracks in the ice shell and "squeeze" these cracks to accelerate the geyser material. See Kite \& Rubin (2016).

To pass the time, she does some astronomy on each leg of the trip. ( $\mathbf{1 0}$ points) When Kirara gets to Ginan, she takes a break on a (fictional) exoplanet orbiting the star. Ginan has a mass of $1.5 M_{\odot}$, and suppose the exoplanet has a mass of $2 M_{\oplus}$, a radius of $1.2 R_{\oplus}$, and a circular orbit with radius 10 AU . She rigs a catapult to give her rocket a one-time boost of $\Delta v$ in any direction. What is the minimum $\Delta v$ required for her to escape the combined gravitational field of both Ginan and the exoplanet?
answer: ( $\mathbf{1 0}$ points) We first compute the gravitational potential at Kirara's location. Assuming her rocket has mass $m$, the gravitational potential energy from Ginan is $$ -\frac{G m\left(1.5 M_{\odot}\right)}{10 \mathrm{AU}}=-\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \cdot\left(1.5 \cdot 1.989 \times 10^{30}\right)}{10 \cdot\left(1.496 \times 10^{11}\right)} m=-\left(1.330 \times 10^{8}\right) m . $$ Similarly, her gravitational potential energy from the exoplanet is $$ -\frac{G m\left(2 M_{\oplus}\right)}{1.2 R_{\oplus}}=-\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \cdot\left(2 \cdot 5.976 \times 10^{24}\right)}{1.2 \cdot\left(6.371 \times 10^{6}\right)} m=-\left(1.043 \times 10^{8}\right) m, $$ so the total gravitational potential energy is $$ -\left(1.330 \times 10^{8}\right) m-\left(1.043 \times 10^{8}\right) m=-\left(2.373 \times 10^{8}\right) m . $$ To escape this gravity well, her kinetic energy must equal her negative potential energy, so we have $\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text {total }}^{2}=\left(2.373 \times 10^{8}\right) m$, so $$ v_{\text {total }}=\sqrt{2 \cdot\left(2.373 \times 10^{8}\right)}=21800 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} . $$ To minimize the $\Delta v$ needed, Kirara should launch in the same direction as the planet's orbit, so we have $v_{\text {total }}=v_{\text {planet }}+\Delta v$, so we need to determine $v_{\text {planet }}$. Since the planet's orbit is circular, we have $M_{\text {planet }} \frac{v_{\text {planet }}^{2}}{R}=\frac{G M_{\text {star }} M_{\text {planet }}}{R^{2}}$, or $$ v_{\text {planet }}=\sqrt{\frac{G M_{\text {star }}}{R}}=\sqrt{\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \cdot\left(1.5 \cdot 1.989 \times 10^{30}\right)}{10 \cdot\left(1.496 \times 10^{11}\right)}}=11533 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} . $$ Thus, the required $\Delta v$ is $(21800 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})-(11533 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})=10300 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

answer: (i) (4 points) Differentiating the magnetic dipole moment twice gives $$ \ddot{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(t)=\mu\left(-\Omega^{2}\sin\chi\cos(\Omega t),-\Omega^{2}\sin\chi\sin(\Omega t),0\right). $$ Therefore, $$ \left|\ddot{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right|=\mu\Omega^{2}\sin\chi . $$ (ii) (5 points) Substituting this into the Larmor formula and using $P=-\dot E$ gives $$ \frac{\mu_{0}}{6\pi c^{3}}\mu^{2}\Omega^{4}\sin^{2}\chi =-I_{z}\Omega\dot{\Omega}, $$ so $$ \dot{\Omega}=-\frac{\mu_{0}}{6\pi c^{3}I_{z}}\mu^{2}\Omega^{3}\sin^{2}\chi . $$ Thus the fixed-$\mu$, fixed-$\chi$ braking index is $n_{0}=3$. (iii) (9 points) Write $$ \dot{\Omega}=-K\mu^{2}\Omega^{3}\sin^{2}\chi, \qquad K=\frac{\mu_{0}}{6\pi c^{3}I_{z}}. $$ Taking a logarithmic time derivative gives $$ \frac{\ddot{\Omega}}{\dot{\Omega}} =2\frac{\dot\mu}{\mu}+3\frac{\dot\Omega}{\Omega}+2\dot\chi\cot\chi . $$ Using $n=\Omega\ddot{\Omega}/\dot{\Omega}^{2}$, $$ n=3+\frac{\Omega}{\dot\Omega} \left(2\frac{\dot\mu}{\mu}+2\dot\chi\cot\chi\right). $$ (iv) (2 points) For $\mu\propto e^{-t/\tau_{B}}$, we have $\dot\mu/\mu=-1/\tau_{B}$, so $$ n=3+\frac{2\Omega}{\dot\Omega} \left(\dot\chi\cot\chi-\frac{1}{\tau_{B}}\right). $$ (v) (7 points) Since $n_{\mathrm{obs}}=2.51<n_{0}=3$ and $\dot\Omega<0$, an increasing $\chi$ shifts the index toward $n_{\mathrm{obs}}$, while a decreasing $\mu$ shifts it away.
